screens.title: Introduction to Exceptions and Error Handling
screens.narratorSegment: In this short module we will learn how Java surfaces unexpected conditions and how your code can respond without crashing. Exceptions are objects created when an event disrupts the normal flow of execution. The runtime searches for a handler and, if none is found, the program terminates. That basic mechanism—throwing an exception and catching it—lets you separate normal logic from recovery logic. You will also learn the important distinction between Error and Exception, and between checked exceptions the compiler forces you to consider and unchecked runtime exceptions that usually signal programming bugs. We will inspect try, catch, and finally blocks, walk through examples for arithmetic errors and command-line division, and highlight common beginner mistakes like swallowing exceptions or catching Exception too broadly. By the end, you will be able to implement basic try-catch patterns, read a stack trace to find the failure point, and make deliberate choices about when to handle an exception and when to let it propagate. Consider what a robust user experience should do instead of failing silently; that idea guides everything we do here.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Introduction
Introduction to Exceptions and Error Handling
Make programs resilient: learn how Java signals and contains failures so applications can recover.
In this lesson
Throwable hierarchy, try-catch-finally, checked vs unchecked, practical examples.
Why it matters
Prevent crashes, give useful feedback, and log the cause for debugging.
Throwable
Superclass of Error and Exception; the root of Java's failure model.
Try-Catch
A controlled way to run code that might fail and react to specific problems.
Stack Trace
A printed call sequence that helps you locate where an exception originated.
Throwable hierarchy (overview)
Throwable → Error | Exception. Exception → checked exceptions and RuntimeException (unchecked).
Quick visual
Error: system-level, usually not recoverable (examples in source include OutOfMemoryError).
Exception: application-level; often something you can catch and handle, like file or input problems.
Explore Key Topics
Throwable hierarchy: root, Error vs Exception, checked vs unchecked.
Try-catch-finally flow: how control moves when an exception is thrown.
Practical examples: arithmetic divide-by-zero and a command-line division utility.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn four practical skills that make Java programs more robust. First, you will differentiate between errors and exceptions: this helps you decide whether a problem should be handled by code or left to the runtime. Second, you will identify the Throwable class hierarchy and learn to recognize checked versus unchecked exceptions so you can respond appropriately. Third, you will implement basic try-catch constructs to handle runtime exceptions gracefully, with an eye toward user-friendly messages and maintainable code. Fourth, you will explain why exception handling matters for reliability, such as avoiding abrupt termination and preserving application state. Each objective is framed as a skill: recognizing the class of failure, choosing whether to handle it, writing the try-catch-finally structure, and producing helpful diagnostics. You will see concrete examples: a divide-by-zero arithmetic failure and a command-line division utility that validates its inputs. As you practice, pay attention to the common mistakes we highlight, like swallowing exceptions or catching Exception too broadly. These objectives prepare you to build resilient Java components and to read stack traces when things go wrong.

screens.title: What is an Exception?
screens.narratorSegment: An exception is an object created when something unexpected disrupts normal program flow. Java methods can create and throw an Exception object when a problem occurs; the runtime then looks for code prepared to handle that object. This mechanism separates normal control flow from error handling, helping you write cleaner code. For example, if code attempts to open a missing file, the file operation throws a checked exception that your method must either catch or declare to rethrow. A concrete example from our chapter is a divide-by-zero; dividing ten by zero triggers an ArithmeticException. A common misconception is that exceptions are only for catastrophic failures. In fact, many are recoverable conditions or require informative messaging for the user. Another common error is treating all exceptions the same: catching the generic superclass hides the real cause and makes debugging hard. The key takeaway is that exceptions are structured signals: they carry a type and a stack trace that point to the failure. Practice by writing small methods that intentionally throw and catch specific exception types so you learn the control flow and the value of precise handlers. How will you decide whether to handle a specific exception or let it propagate?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › What is an Exception?
Exception — formal definition
An object created when the normal flow is interrupted; it can be thrown and caught by handlers.
• Carries a type that identifies the failure (for example, ArithmeticException).
• Includes a stack trace that shows the call sequence at the time it was thrown.
• Can be handled by matching catch blocks or allowed to propagate up the call stack.
Concrete example
Divide ten by zero: Java creates an ArithmeticException and halts the try block, then looks for a matching catch to run recovery code.
Key Takeaway

Treat exceptions as structured signals: type + stack trace. Handle specific types to preserve context for debugging.

Common misconception
Believing all exceptions are fatal. Many can be handled to recover or to present a helpful error to the user. Distinguish recoverable exceptions from system Errors.
Analogy
Think of an exception as an alarm with details: the alarm type tells you the problem class and the attached log points to where it started.
Check your understanding
If a method throws an exception you do not catch, what happens? The runtime searches the caller chain for a handler; if none exists, the program terminates and prints the stack trace.

screens.title: Error vs Exception
screens.narratorSegment: Java groups all failures under Throwable, but not all failures are equal. An Error represents serious conditions often external to the application, like the runtime running out of memory or a stack overflow. Because these signal defects in the environment or the JVM, applications generally should not try to catch them. An Exception, by contrast, represents conditions an application might reasonably handle: missing files, invalid user input, or recoverable input and output problems. Within Exception we split into checked and unchecked categories. Checked exceptions are enforced by the compiler: you must catch them or declare that your method throws them. This forces you to think about potential failure points—for example, file operations often throw IOException. Unchecked exceptions, subclasses of RuntimeException, usually indicate programming mistakes such as null references or invalid array indexes. A common mistake is catching Error or catching Exception at the top level to hide problems; this can make debugging impossible. Instead, choose narrow handlers for known, recoverable conditions and allow catastrophic Errors to surface. Which failures in your application are recoverable and which should fail fast? Error vs Exception means errors are severe and usually not recoverable; exceptions are application conditions you can often handle. choose handlers accordingly.. In practical terms, when to catch and when to let the jvm handle it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Error vs Exception
Error
Severe conditions you generally should not catch. Examples include OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError mentioned in the chapter.
  • • External to normal application control.
  • • Often indicate JVM or system resource failure.
  • • Recovery is rarely feasible by application code.
Common mistake: trying to catch Errors to hide failure; this may mask the real system issue.
Exception
Application-level conditions you can often catch and handle. Split into checked and unchecked exceptions.
  • • Checked exceptions: compiler forces you to catch or declare (for example IOException).
  • • Unchecked exceptions: RuntimeException subclasses like NullPointerException or ArithmeticException.
Best practice: catch specific exceptions you can recover from; log or rethrow others.
Why it matters
Correct classification prevents hiding critical system failures and ensures recoverable issues get handled.
Pro tip
Use narrow catches and meaningful logs instead of catching Exception broadly.
Check
Ask: Can this failure be recovered from without restarting the JVM?

screens.title: try, catch, finally — control flow
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the control flow for try, catch, and finally is essential. When execution enters a try block it runs until either completion or a thrown exception. If no exception occurs the catch blocks are skipped and finally executes if present. If an exception is thrown, the try block stops immediately and the runtime searches the associated catch blocks for the first type that matches the thrown exception. If a matching catch is found, its code runs; after the catch, the finally block runs if present, and execution continues after the try-catch-finally construct. If no catch matches, the exception propagates up the call stack to the caller, repeating the search there. A concrete scenario: dividing by zero inside a try triggers ArithmeticException; a catch for ArithmeticException runs recovery and finally still runs for cleanup. A common misconception is that finally only runs when no exception occurs; in fact finally runs in both normal and exceptional paths. Another trap is assuming catch order doesn't matter; because catches are checked top to bottom, a broad catch placed before a specific one will prevent the specific handler from running. When you write handlers, ensure the most specific exceptions appear first and use finally for guaranteed cleanup.

keyIdea.title: Control flow
keyIdea.text: Thrown exceptions abort the try and jump to the first matching catch; finally always runs for cleanup regardless of success or exception.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › try-catch-finally
Execution steps
1. Enter try and execute statements sequentially.
2. If a statement throws, abort the try and search catch blocks for a matching type.
3. Run the matching catch. If none found, propagate the exception upward.
4. Execute finally whether or not an exception occurred, then continue after the construct.
Specific vs broad catches
Place specific exception types before broader ones. A catch for Exception placed before a specific type will prevent the specific handler from ever running.
Key Takeaway

finally is the guaranteed cleanup block. Use it for closing resources even when exceptions occur.

Example scenario
Try to divide by zero inside try: ArithmeticException is thrown, matching catch runs, finally runs, and program continues after the block.
Check your understanding
What happens if finally throws a new exception while handling another? The new exception propagates, potentially replacing the original; avoid throwing from finally when possible.

screens.title: BasicExceptionHandling example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the provided BasicExceptionHandling example so you can see the mechanism in action. The program sets a numerator and a denominator where the denominator is zero. The division line is inside a try block; when execution reaches that division, the runtime detects an attempt to divide by zero and throws an ArithmeticException. The catch block specifically catches ArithmeticException and prints a user-friendly error message to the standard error stream, then prints the stack trace. Printing the stack trace is important because it shows the method calls leading to the exception, which is essential for debugging. After the catch block completes, the finally block executes, which prints a message indicating the try-catch has finished. The program then continues with subsequent statements after the try-catch-finally. A common mistake is to print only a brief message and not log the stack trace; doing so reduces your ability to diagnose where the problem started. Another mistake is catching Exception too generally. Prefer catching ArithmeticException when you know this particular failure can occur and you can respond meaningfully. How would you change the handler if you wanted to retry with a nonzero denominator?

keyIdea.text: Catching a specific exception lets you give a helpful message and still retain the diagnostic stack trace for debugging.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › BasicExceptionHandling
Code example
public class BasicExceptionHandling {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    int numerator = 10;
    int denominator = 0; // This will cause an ArithmeticException

    try {
      int result = numerator / denominator; // Potential exception point
      System.out.println("Result: " + result);
    } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
      System.err.println("An arithmetic error occurred: " + e.getMessage());
      System.err.println("Please ensure the denominator is not zero.");
      e.printStackTrace();
    } finally {
      System.out.println("Execution of try-catch block finished.");
    }
    System.out.println("Program continues after the try-catch block.");
  }
}
Walkthrough
The division throws ArithmeticException; the catch prints helpful messages and the stack trace; finally always runs.
Common mistake
Only printing a short message without the stack trace makes debugging much harder. Always log diagnostic details in addition to user-friendly messages.
Try this

Modify the handler to prompt for a new denominator and retry instead of exiting, if that makes sense for your program.

screens.title: DivisionCalculator starter code
screens.narratorSegment: The DivisionCalculator task reinforces handling several exception types in one small program. The starter code first checks args length and prints usage if fewer than two arguments are provided. If the arguments exist, parsing them to integers may throw NumberFormatException when the strings are not valid integers. After parsing, performing division can throw ArithmeticException if the denominator is zero. The chapter suggests catching NumberFormatException and ArithmeticException and printing user-friendly errors while also printing the stack trace for diagnostics. It also notes that attempting to access args[0] or args[1] without verifying args. length could throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, which you can avoid by checking length first. In practice, you should check args length, then use a try-catch around parsing and division with separate catches for NumberFormatException and ArithmeticException, both of which should log the stack trace to help debugging. This pattern shows a real program-level decision: validate early, handle specific exceptions to give precise feedback, and always keep enough diagnostic detail to fix the root cause. When you implement this, think about whether it makes sense to retry, prompt, or exit gracefully depending on the application context.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › DivisionCalculator
Starter code
public class DivisionCalculator {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    if (args.length < 2) {
      System.err.println("Usage: java DivisionCalculator <number1> <number2>");
      System.err.println("Please provide two integer arguments.");
      return;
    }

    int num1 = 0;
    int num2 = 0;

    try {
      num1 = Integer.parseInt(args[0]);
      num2 = Integer.parseInt(args[1]);
      int result = num1 / num2;
      System.out.println("Result of " + num1 + " / " + num2 + " = " + result);

    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
      System.err.println("Error: Invalid number format provided.");
      e.printStackTrace();
    } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
      System.err.println("Error: Cannot divide by zero.");
      e.printStackTrace();
    }

    System.out.println("Calculation attempt finished.");
  }
}
Error conditions to handle
• Missing arguments: check args.length first. • Invalid integer input: NumberFormatException. • Division by zero: ArithmeticException.
Best practice
Validate early, give clear user errors, and log the stack trace for debugging. Avoid catching Exception broadly.
Try this

Extend the program to ask for new input instead of exiting when the user provides invalid data, if interactive behavior is acceptable.

screens.title: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions
screens.narratorSegment: A central Java design decision is the split between checked and unchecked exceptions. Checked exceptions are those the compiler requires you to acknowledge: if a method can throw a checked exception, you must either catch it or declare the method throws it. Common examples are IO-related failures such as IOException. This compiler-enforced handling makes you confront potential failure points early in development and document which operations can fail. Unchecked exceptions are subclasses of RuntimeException and are not enforced by the compiler. These often indicate programming errors such as null references, invalid array access, or arithmetic errors. The rationale is that unchecked exceptions usually signal bugs that should be fixed rather than routinely caught. A common misconception is that checked exceptions are always better because they force handling; in practice, overusing checked exceptions can clutter code if thrown for routine control flow. The practical rule of thumb in this chapter: use checked exceptions for expected, recoverable conditions that callers should handle; use unchecked exceptions for programmer errors that require code fixes. When writing handlers, prefer specific catches for these types so callers can respond appropriately.

keyIdea.title: Compiler role
keyIdea.text: Checked exceptions force explicit handling at compile time; unchecked exceptions indicate programming bugs and are optional to catch.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Checked vs Unchecked
Checked Exceptions
Examples include file and database operations such as IOException and SQLException. The compiler forces you to catch or declare these so callers consider recovery.
• Use when callers should be made aware of and handle expected failures.
Unchecked Exceptions
RuntimeException subclasses like NullPointerException, ArithmeticException, and ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. These often indicate programmer errors and are not required to be declared or caught.
• Use unchecked for bugs that should be fixed rather than routinely handled at runtime.
Why it matters
Choosing checked vs unchecked shapes API design and caller responsibilities.
Misconception
Checked exceptions are not always preferable; avoid using them for normal control flow.
Practice
Classify example types from the chapter into checked or unchecked categories to reinforce the difference.

screens.title: Common mistakes: swallowing and broad catches
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often make two interrelated mistakes when handling exceptions that greatly reduce maintainability. The first is swallowing exceptions: catching an exception and doing nothing or printing only a vague message. When you swallow an exception, you throw away context that would help diagnose the failure later. The chapter warns against merely printing an error string without the stack trace. The second mistake is catching Exception too broadly. A top-level catch for Exception will match nearly every problem and can hide specific issues like null references or input and output failures, making it hard to apply appropriate recovery or to notice systemic problems. A better pattern is to catch narrow, expected exception types and log the stack trace so you retain a record of the call sequence. If you must have a broad handler at a high level for logging and graceful shutdown, ensure it logs detailed diagnostics and does not silently hide the condition. The overall rule: provide useful feedback to the user and preserve debugging information for developers. How will you ensure your handlers remain informative without obscuring root causes?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Common mistakes
Swallowing exceptions
Catching an exception and doing nothing or only printing a vague message removes the context needed for debugging.
• Always log the stack trace or sufficient diagnostic data. • Provide user-friendly guidance while keeping developer logs detailed.
Catching Exception too broadly
A broad catch can hide the real problem and prevent specific recovery actions for known issues.
• Catch specific types first. • Use a single top-level broad handler only for logging and graceful shutdown.

Silent catches and overly broad handlers make it hard to reproduce and fix defects. Preserve context.

Write small, specific handlers and centralize logging so you keep a clear record of what went wrong and where.

screens.title: Stack Trace — your primary debugging aid
screens.narratorSegment: When an exception goes unhandled or when you call printStackTrace, Java emits a stack trace — a list of active method calls at the moment the exception was thrown. The stack trace usually begins with the exception type and the message, followed by a sequence of lines showing each method, class, and source line number. This is the quickest way to find where an error originated. For example, in the divide-by-zero scenario, the trace shows the line where division happened and the call chain that led there. A common beginner mistake is to ignore the stack trace or rely only on the error message. Because many exceptions share similar messages, the trace provides the exact file and line to inspect. Use the trace to find the method to fix or to check whether you should add a handler. When logging exceptions, include the full stack trace rather than only a summary string. Practice reading traces from the examples in this chapter to build intuition about how upstream calls propagate exceptions. What does the top-most stack frame tell you about where to look first?

screens.narratorSegment: The chapter includes a small assessment snippet that shows how catching specific exceptions leads to predictable program output. When a program accesses args[0] without providing command-line arguments, Java throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. In the provided example MyClass, the code prints args[0] inside a try and has a catch for ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException followed by a catch for Exception. Running the program with no arguments triggers the first catch, which prints a clear message and lets the program continue. Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Assessment: Missing Args
Assessment snippet
public class MyClass {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    try {
      System.out.println(args[0]);
    } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
      System.out.println("Error: No argument provided.");
    } catch (Exception e) {
      System.out.println("An unexpected error occurred.");
    }
    System.out.println("Program finished.");
  }
}
Correct answer
It prints the array index error message and then "Program finished." because the specific ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException is caught first.
Reflection
Decide if proactive argument validation or exception handling is more appropriate based on user expectations and program context.

screens.title: Design choices and when to rethrow
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond catching exceptions locally, you must design how failures propagate through your A P I. If a method cannot resolve a problem, it can declare throws and let the caller decide how to handle the exception. This is common with checked exceptions like IOException; the low-level method declares the exception and higher-level code either catches and handles it or further declares it. Rethrowing is also a deliberate choice: you may catch an exception to add context or to log, and then rethrow to preserve caller responsibility. When rethrowing, consider attaching a clear message about what failed so stack traces carry helpful context. The chapter cautions against blanket catches that both hide and swallow errors. Use logging to record full stack traces at the point where you understand the failure best. If an exception represents a programmer bug (unchecked), prefer fixing the code rather than catching it repeatedly. When building libraries, document which exceptions callers should expect and handle. This clear contract helps avoid surprises and keeps error handling consistent across components. Which exceptions should your A P I surface, and which should it handle internally?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Design & Rethrow
When to declare throws
If the current code cannot reasonably resolve the failure, declare throws and document the expectation for callers to handle it.
Example: a file-reading method can declare IOException, letting higher-level code decide whether to retry, prompt, or exit.
Rethrow with context
Catch to add helpful context or to log, then rethrow the exception so the caller still sees the original failure and stack trace.
Avoid losing the original exception. When wrapping, include the original exception as the cause.
Key Takeaway

Design exception behavior as part of your API contract: surface what callers must handle, handle what you can, and always keep diagnostic detail for debugging.

In this short module we will learn how Java surfaces unexpected conditions and how your code can respond without crashing. Exceptions are objects created when an event disrupts the normal flow of execution. The runtime searches for a handler and, if none is found, the program terminates. That basic mechanism—throwing an exception and catching it—lets you separate normal logic from recovery logic. You will also learn the important distinction between Error and Exception, and between checked exceptions the compiler forces you to consider and unchecked runtime exceptions that usually signal programming bugs. We will inspect try, catch, and finally blocks, walk through examples for arithmetic errors and command-line division, and highlight common beginner mistakes like swallowing exceptions or catching Exception too broadly. By the end, you will be able to implement basic try-catch patterns, read a stack trace to find the failure point, and make deliberate choices about when to handle an exception and when to let it propagate. Consider what a robust user experience should do instead of failing silently; that idea guides everything we do here.

In this lesson you will learn four practical skills that make Java programs more robust. First, you will differentiate between errors and exceptions: this helps you decide whether a problem should be handled by code or left to the runtime. Second, you will identify the Throwable class hierarchy and learn to recognize checked versus unchecked exceptions so you can respond appropriately. Third, you will implement basic try-catch constructs to handle runtime exceptions gracefully, with an eye toward user-friendly messages and maintainable code. Fourth, you will explain why exception handling matters for reliability, such as avoiding abrupt termination and preserving application state. Each objective is framed as a skill: recognizing the class of failure, choosing whether to handle it, writing the try-catch-finally structure, and producing helpful diagnostics. You will see concrete examples: a divide-by-zero arithmetic failure and a command-line division utility that validates its inputs. As you practice, pay attention to the common mistakes we highlight, like swallowing exceptions or catching Exception too broadly. These objectives prepare you to build resilient Java components and to read stack traces when things go wrong.

This second objectives screen focuses on applying and validating the same four learning targets through concrete practice. First, when differentiating Error and Exception, you will examine examples like out-of-memory issues versus recoverable file or input errors so you can decide when to handle or let the JVM escalate. Second, identifying the Throwable hierarchy becomes practical when you classify sample types such as IOException and ArithmeticException into checked or unchecked buckets. Third, you will implement try-catch and finally blocks in small programs, ensuring resource cleanup and user-friendly error messages instead of abrupt crashes. Fourth, to demonstrate the importance of exception handling, you will run a command-line division utility that handles invalid input, missing arguments, and division-by-zero without terminating unexpectedly. For each step you will also learn one common mistake and a quick practice to check understanding, for example avoiding catching Exception too broadly and never swallowing exceptions without logging. These applied milestones help you move from concept to reliable code and prepare you for the hands-on activity in the chapter.

An exception is an object created when something unexpected disrupts normal program flow. Java methods can create and throw an Exception object when a problem occurs; the runtime then looks for code prepared to handle that object. This mechanism separates normal control flow from error handling, helping you write cleaner code. For example, if code attempts to open a missing file, the file operation throws a checked exception that your method must either catch or declare to rethrow. A concrete example from our chapter is a divide-by-zero; dividing ten by zero triggers an ArithmeticException. A common misconception is that exceptions are only for catastrophic failures. In fact, many are recoverable conditions or require informative messaging for the user. Another common error is treating all exceptions the same: catching the generic superclass hides the real cause and makes debugging hard. The key takeaway is that exceptions are structured signals: they carry a type and a stack trace that point to the failure. Practice by writing small methods that intentionally throw and catch specific exception types so you learn the control flow and the value of precise handlers. How will you decide whether to handle a specific exception or let it propagate?

Java groups all failures under Throwable, but not all failures are equal. An Error represents serious conditions often external to the application, like the runtime running out of memory or a stack overflow. Because these signal defects in the environment or the JVM, applications generally should not try to catch them. An Exception, by contrast, represents conditions an application might reasonably handle: missing files, invalid user input, or recoverable input and output problems. Within Exception we split into checked and unchecked categories. Checked exceptions are enforced by the compiler: you must catch them or declare that your method throws them. This forces you to think about potential failure points—for example, file operations often throw IOException. Unchecked exceptions, subclasses of RuntimeException, usually indicate programming mistakes such as null references or invalid array indexes. A common mistake is catching Error or catching Exception at the top level to hide problems; this can make debugging impossible. Instead, choose narrow handlers for known, recoverable conditions and allow catastrophic Errors to surface. Which failures in your application are recoverable and which should fail fast? Error vs Exception means errors are severe and usually not recoverable; exceptions are application conditions you can often handle. choose handlers accordingly.. In practical terms, when to catch and when to let the jvm handle it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the control flow for try, catch, and finally is essential. When execution enters a try block it runs until either completion or a thrown exception. If no exception occurs the catch blocks are skipped and finally executes if present. If an exception is thrown, the try block stops immediately and the runtime searches the associated catch blocks for the first type that matches the thrown exception. If a matching catch is found, its code runs; after the catch, the finally block runs if present, and execution continues after the try-catch-finally construct. If no catch matches, the exception propagates up the call stack to the caller, repeating the search there. A concrete scenario: dividing by zero inside a try triggers ArithmeticException; a catch for ArithmeticException runs recovery and finally still runs for cleanup. A common misconception is that finally only runs when no exception occurs; in fact finally runs in both normal and exceptional paths. Another trap is assuming catch order doesn't matter; because catches are checked top to bottom, a broad catch placed before a specific one will prevent the specific handler from running. When you write handlers, ensure the most specific exceptions appear first and use finally for guaranteed cleanup.

Let's walk through the provided BasicExceptionHandling example so you can see the mechanism in action. The program sets a numerator and a denominator where the denominator is zero. The division line is inside a try block; when execution reaches that division, the runtime detects an attempt to divide by zero and throws an ArithmeticException. The catch block specifically catches ArithmeticException and prints a user-friendly error message to the standard error stream, then prints the stack trace. Printing the stack trace is important because it shows the method calls leading to the exception, which is essential for debugging. After the catch block completes, the finally block executes, which prints a message indicating the try-catch has finished. The program then continues with subsequent statements after the try-catch-finally. A common mistake is to print only a brief message and not log the stack trace; doing so reduces your ability to diagnose where the problem started. Another mistake is catching Exception too generally. Prefer catching ArithmeticException when you know this particular failure can occur and you can respond meaningfully. How would you change the handler if you wanted to retry with a nonzero denominator?

The DivisionCalculator task reinforces handling several exception types in one small program. The starter code first checks args length and prints usage if fewer than two arguments are provided. After parsing, performing division can throw ArithmeticException if the denominator is zero. The chapter suggests catching NumberFormatException and ArithmeticException and printing user-friendly errors while also printing the stack trace for diagnostics. In practice, you should check args length, then use a try-catch around parsing and division with separate catches for NumberFormatException and ArithmeticException, both of which should log the stack trace to help debugging. This pattern shows a real program-level decision: validate early, handle specific exceptions to give precise feedback, and always keep enough diagnostic detail to fix the root cause. When you implement this, think about whether it makes sense to retry, prompt, or exit gracefully depending on the application context.
